scope.description: Hand-researched deepening pass for Japanese Rocket Gang and seven rows that carry the set's dark-variant, trainer, and energy structure.

sources.title: Local Japanese pre-English catalog: Rocket Gang
TCGdex API set record: PMCG4 Rocket Gang

claims.text: The local catalog models Rocket Gang as released on November 21, 1997.
The local catalog, Pokellector, TCGdex snapshot, and Bulbapedia all support a 65-card Japanese Rocket Gang checklist.
Bulbapedia identifies Rocket Gang as the fourth main Japanese Pokemon Card Game expansion and the Japanese counterpart named on the English Team Rocket page.
Bulbapedia describes Team Rocket / Rocket Gang as introducing Dark Pokemon as a card type with a distinct visual treatment and different HP/attack character from normal Pokemon cards.
The local symbol-status matrix records Rocket Gang as printing with rarity symbols, so Rocket Gang is not a Base No Rarity source.

The local catalog models Japanese Rocket Gang as 65 rows; English Team Rocket has a different row count and includes English-only secret-number logic that must not be imported into this Japanese release dossier.
The local Rocket Gang attention rows include Dark Charizard, Dark Blastoise, Dark Gyarados, Dark Dragonite, Rocket's Sneak Attack, Here Comes Team Rocket!, and Rainbow Energy.
The local Rocket Gang artist clusters are led by Kagemaru Himeno, Mitsuhiro Arita, Ken Sugimori, Sumiyoshi Kizuki, Atsuko Nishida, and several smaller contributor clusters.

Rocket Gang matters because it makes ownership visible as a design language: familiar Kanto Pokemon return under a darker frame, while trainer and energy holos make the villain theme feel like a whole apparatus rather than a few mascot cards.

special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, slab label, or agent search says Rocket Gang, Japanese Team Rocket, PMCG4, Dark Pokemon, Dark Charizard, or Team Rocket secret card.
special_identification_instructions.summary: Rocket Gang is the 65-row Japanese release; keep it separate from English Team Rocket and from the later Team Rocket Gift Pack deck-component context.
steps: Preserve release_family_id jp_tcg_rocket_gang_19971121 for the Japanese booster release.
Do not import English Team Rocket row numbers, English-only secret-card framing, or Dark Raichu 83/82 logic into Japanese Rocket Gang.
Do not collapse Rocket Gang into Team Rocket Gift Pack; the gift product is a separate release context built from Rocket Gang material.
Do not treat Rocket Gang as a Base No Rarity source; the symbol-status matrix marks this release as printing with rarity symbols.
When a card is described only as Dark Charizard, Dark Blastoise, or another Dark Pokemon, ask for language, set, row number, and image evidence before resolving the exact release.
not_claiming: Team Rocket Gift Pack sealed-unit contents

narrative.human_title: When the binder learns who owns the Pokemon
narrative.why_it_matters: Rocket Gang is the set where the card game lets the story darken without leaving the table. The Pokemon are still Kanto bodies a collector recognizes, but the frame changes the relationship: these are creatures seen through Team Rocket's hands. That is why the set feels bigger than a villain logo. It teaches the catalog to track ownership, mood, numbering, and release language before trusting the familiar silhouette.

Dark Charizard matters because Charizard already carries early Pokemon gravity, and Rocket Gang reframes that gravity as a darker ownership story.

narrative.human_title: The famous silhouette under worse weather
narrative.why_it_matters: Dark Charizard is the obvious gravity well, which is exactly why the dossier has to stay sober. The card is not important only because Charizard is famous; it is important because Rocket Gang changes the moral lighting around the most familiar fire silhouette in the room. The agent should feel the pull, then ask for the row.

narrative.human_title: The heavy starter turned toward Rocket
narrative.why_it_matters: Dark Blastoise is Rocket Gang's weight. The cannons are already there in the collector's memory, but Arita's row lets the set point that weight in a more suspicious direction. It is familiar enough to trust at a glance and altered enough that the glance should not be trusted.

narrative.human_title: The monster with a last spark
narrative.why_it_matters: Dark Gyarados is where Rocket Gang feels less like a costume and more like temperament. Himeno's row carries the familiar sea-serpent dread, but the local metadata's Final Beam idea gives it a spiteful little afterimage. It is not just darker in color; it behaves like something mishandled.

narrative.why_it_matters: Dark Dragonite is quietly weird in the best way. Dragonite usually reads as gentle mass, mail-route kindness, rounded power. Rocket Gang gives it a minion-summoning role, and Arita's credit keeps that shift attached to one of the strongest early visual hands in the game. The card is lovable, but the set makes it organized.

narrative.human_title: The villains step onto the holo stage
narrative.why_it_matters: Rocket's Sneak Attack is the moment the set stops only darkening Pokemon and lets Team Rocket act directly. Sugimori's credit makes it feel like a piece of franchise staging: a trainer card with the same theatrical charge as the monsters around it. The apparatus has people in it.

Here Comes Team Rocket! matters because the local row shows a common-rarity trainer with holo-source signal, making the set's theatrical villain entrance a structural card rather than only flavor text.

narrative.why_it_matters: Here Comes Team Rocket! is wonderfully blunt. It does not hide the theme behind a Dark prefix; it opens the door and says the villains are here. The local common-plus-holo nuance makes it a good agent test: preserve the weirdness, do not smooth it into a generic rare-looking trainer.

narrative.human_title: The set's machine has color in it
narrative.why_it_matters: Rainbow Energy is the reminder that Rocket Gang is not only about darkened creatures. The set reaches into the resource layer: the thing that pays for action becomes collectible, shiny, and weirdly central. Akabane's credit makes this feel less like a background utility and more like a small machine part worth cataloging carefully.
